question: A worked example of every page type: a fictional regional rail operator, Northvale Rail, asks whether and how it can grow from 48 million to 60 million journeys a year by FY31. Every number is illustrative.
answer: Northvale can reach 60 million journeys by FY31 by filling the off-peak rather than the full peak: add off-peak frequency first, electrify the Eastern line next and reform fares last.

textPlan.text: Northvale can reach 60 million journeys by FY31 by filling the off-peak
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator
Crews and units released from the peak
Journeys recovered to 48.3 million in FY26 but growth slowed to 1.7%: peak trains run above 90% of their seats, so the peak cannot absorb the 11.7 million extra journeys.
Off-peak trains run at 38% of their seats. Half-hourly stations grew off-peak journeys 3.7 times as fast as hourly ones, so frequency, not fares, is the main lever.
Electrifying the Eastern line costs £390 million, beats bi-mode trains on cost per journey from year six and frees diesel units for the Dales line.
The £640 million plan pays back in eleven years on the central case, if the power upgrade lands by 2029 and punctuality holds at 90%.

Source: illustrative data for fictional operators; route-km excludes freight-only track
Northvale carries 104 thousand journeys per route-km, just under the peer median of 108 and 27% below Westmoor, the most intensive operator in the set.
Westmoor and Southdown run half-hourly off-peak services on most lines; Northvale runs hourly on three of its five, and its peak intensity is close to theirs.
Reaching the peer median off-peak intensity on the Dales and Valley lines alone would add about 7 million journeys a year on today's network.

Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 on-train survey, 11,400 responses
Journeys by purpose and time band, FY26,
Commuters are 68% of peak journeys but 18% of weekday off-peak journeys, where leisure trips make up two thirds of travel.
A leisure trip can go by car or not happen at all, so it responds to waiting time and reach far more than a commute does.
Growth between the peaks is a leisure product: frequency, weekend service and destinations, not a cheaper season ticket.

textPlan.text: Half-hourly off-peak stations grew off-peak journeys 3.7 times as fast as hourly ones
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; ticket sales by origin station
Off-peak service against off-peak journey growth, FY23-FY26
The six stations with 30 or more off-peak trains a weekday grew off-peak journeys by 16.5% on average over three years; the four stations still served hourly grew by 4.5%.
Population grew by 2-4% around all ten stations over the same period, so it cannot explain a gap of twelve points between the two groups.
Growth rises steeply up to about 30 trains a day and flattens after it: a half-hourly service is the threshold that matters, and more than that adds little off-peak demand.

At £17.60 per train-km Northvale sits just below the field's median of £18.10, and £3.40 above Westmoor, the lowest-cost operator.
Five of the six lowest-cost operators run electric trains on their busiest lines; every operator above £19.00 still runs diesel on most of its network.
Electric trains on the Eastern line take Northvale to £16.40 by FY31, which would place it sixth on today's figures.

pages.claim: Each peak train added to the Eastern line has cost a point of punctuality

settles.what: Eastern line peak trains per hour and punctuality, FY19-FY26

pages.adds: The points give the mechanism - dwell time at single-track sections - and why the off-peak does not share it

textPlan.text: Each peak train added to the Eastern line has cost a point of punctuality
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; punctuality is arrivals within five minutes

Four extra peak trains an hour since FY22 have coincided with a 5.1-point fall in Eastern line punctuality: each added train leaves less recovery time at the two single-track sections east of Selby, so one late train now delays the next three.
Off-peak trains share none of that conflict, because the single-track sections are free for most of the hour between the peaks.
The plan therefore holds the peak timetable where it is and adds all its new service between the peaks, where it costs no punctuality.

pages.claim: Three constraints hold the peak where it is: fleet, track and depot

settles.what: units in peak service, single-track sections and depot sidings in use, FY26

pages.adds: Each row says what binds, where it binds and what lifting it would take, beyond the number at its right

textPlan.text: Three constraints hold the peak where it is: fleet, track and depot
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; fleet diagram, track layout and depot plan, FY26
single-track sections on the Eastern line
All 58 units run in the morning peak and none is held spare, so a failure cancels a train rather than swapping in a replacement.
New units are on order but not before 2029, when electrification releases eleven diesel units for other lines.
The Eastern line runs through two single-track sections where trains in opposite directions wait for each other.
Each extra peak train adds a crossing, which is why punctuality fell as the timetable grew.
Doubling both sections would cost about £38 million and is not in the funded plan.
The Dales depot stables trains overnight in 94% of its sidings, so no more units can be based there.
The planned extension adds twelve sidings for £55 million and is the one dependency of the off-peak timetable.

Walkers and day-trippers who decide the day before; they need a later last train home, not a faster one.

textPlan.text: London and Manchester send three in five of the visitors from beyond the network
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; FY26 ticket sales by origin station
Three in five from two cities
London and Manchester send 1.46 million of the 2.45 million visitor journeys a year that start beyond the network, most of them bound for the Dales and the coast.
Nearly all of these visitors change at Leeds from an intercity train, so the connection there decides whether the trip continues by rail or by hire car.
Aligning the half-hourly Dales service with the London and Manchester arrivals cuts the average wait at Leeds from 31 minutes to 12.
The demand model credits through tickets and timed connections with 0.8 million of the 5.1 million journeys the off-peak timetable adds.

textPlan.text: The plan adds 11.7 million journeys a year by FY31, mostly after electrification
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; demand model central case
Electrified Eastern trains start to add journeys
Growth runs at 2.7% a year until FY28, while the Dales and Valley timetables bed in, and then at about 5% a year as electrified Eastern trains enter service and fare reform launches.
Six of the 11.7 million journeys arrive in FY30 and FY31, so the target is exposed to any slip in the power-supply upgrade due in 2029.
On the low case the path flattens after FY29 and ends at 56.5 million: the timetable levers still deliver, electrification does not.

pages.claim: Fare reform should follow the new timetable, not lead it

settles.what: why fare reform should follow the timetable change rather than lead it

textPlan.text: Fare reform should follow the new timetable, not lead it
Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator; fare elasticity from the demand model

Cheaper off-peak fares are the obvious lever, and the one most often proposed. On Northvale's evidence they are the weaker one: lapsed riders cite the wait for the next train twice as often as the fare, and the Coast line, which already sells the cheapest off-peak day return on the network, has the lowest off-peak growth.

A fare cut on an hourly service mostly discounts trips that would have been made anyway. The same cut on a half-hourly service reaches riders who have just been given a reason to come back, and the revenue it gives up is partly repaid by the extra journeys.

So the order matters. Run the new Dales and Valley timetables for a full year, measure who they bring back, and then design the part-time season ticket and the off-peak return around the travel patterns that result. Introduced first, fare reform would cost an estimated £6 million a year in lost revenue for about 0.4 million journeys; introduced second, it adds 1.6 million journeys for the same cost.

pages.claim: Four decisions put Northvale on the path to 60 million journeys

settles.what: the four decisions the plan asks of the board

textPlan.text: Four decisions put Northvale on the path to 60 million journeys
Approve the Dales and Valley half-hourly off-peak timetables for December 2027 and May 2028.
Commit £390 million to electrify the Eastern line, with bi-mode trains as the fallback.
Hold fare reform until the new timetables have run for a year, then launch in 2030.
Hold the peak timetable and a 90% punctuality floor while train-km rise by a fifth.
